Triggers.value: Beginning to feel detached or unreal

Maladaptive Strategies.value: keep mind occupied all the time

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

vignette:
Adebayo sits stiffly in the chair, his long fingers laced together on his lap. At seventy-seven, he carries himself with a quiet dignity that seems at odds with the turmoil he has finally come to describe. For over fifty years, he has carried the memory of the day the soldiers came. It doesn't play like a film in his mind; he explains that it never has. Instead, it exists as a series of silent, stark photographs. There is the image of his neighbour’s door splintering. There is a close-up of a dusty boot on his family’s prayer mat. And there is the face of a young man, no older than his own son is now, holding a rifle, his expression a blank slate of authority. When Adebayo speaks of these moments, his voice is unnervingly steady, almost clinical. He reports the details as if they happened to a stranger, a character in a book he once read, a complete absence of emotion hollowing out the words. This numbness is, in its own way, as frightening as the images themselves.

After escaping the civil war and rebuilding his life in America as a software engineer, Adebayo believed he had left that day behind. He married his wife, Funke, raised a family, and found a certain peace in the clean logic of code. Yet, the past was never truly gone. It lived in the periphery, waiting for a crack to seep through. The triggers are often mundane. Last month, during a team meeting at the tech firm where he still consults, his project manager, a well-meaning woman half his age, gave a direct instruction about a deadline. "Adebayo, I need you to drop everything else and have this module debugged by noon." The tone was not harsh, but the command—the simple act of being given an order—sent a jolt through him. The air in the conference room seemed to thin, the voices of his colleagues receding into a distant hum. It was the beginning of that familiar, terrifying feeling of detachment, as if he were floating a few inches above his own body, watching a stranger nod in agreement.

To manage these moments, Adebayo has, over the years, built a fortress of avoidance around himself. He now works almost exclusively from home, limiting his interactions to emails and carefully scheduled calls. He knows this has created distance with his younger colleagues, but the risk of a face-to-face command is too great. His world has been shrinking in other ways, too. Funke’s invitations to community gatherings or even dinner with friends are met with polite, but firm, refusals. He explains that he is tired, that he has a complex coding problem he needs to solve. The truth is, the thought of navigating a crowd, of unpredictable social demands, is unbearable. He feels safest in his study, his mind wholly consumed by the intricate patterns of software architecture. He has come to rely on this intense mental focus as a shield; as long as he is untangling a logical knot, there is no room for the silent photographs to appear. He must keep his mind occupied at all times.

The decision to seek help came after a conversation with Funke two weeks ago. She had found him staring blankly at a news report about a conflict in another country, his hands trembling slightly. She sat beside him, her presence a quiet accusation of his absence. "I feel I am losing you, Ade," she had said, her voice soft but heavy with years of unspoken worry. "You are here, but you are not. It is like you are living in a room no one else can enter." Her words breached his carefully constructed numbness. He saw the pain in her eyes and realized his strategies for survival were costing him the very life he had fought so hard to build. He is here now, not because the memories are worse, but because his isolation has finally become more frightening than they are. He is terrified of dredging up the past, but he is more terrified of a future spent alone inside his own head, a silent observer of a life he is no longer truly living.
